sentences.text: Last time, we pooled all five clinics into a single standard.
Drawn on the log-odds ruler, that standard is one line: lower-risk patients start at 23%, and higher risk is one step up, to 63%.
Now put the clinics back.
Alder's patients sit above the line, at both ends. So do Dune's.
Birch and Cedar sit below it, at both ends. And Elm, with no readmissions at all, is off the bottom of the chart.
One line for everyone misses, and it misses clinic by clinic.
So here is today's question: what is the smallest change that fixes it?
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: one intercept per provider.
The obvious fix is to give every clinic a line of its own: its own starting point, and its own step.
That's what we did for Cedar, two episodes ago.
But look at what it costs.
Each line now rests on one clinic's patients alone. Alder's higher-risk end is just 6 people.
And the gap between two clinics is no longer one number. Alder sits further above Cedar for higher-risk patients than for lower-risk ones.
So the question 'how much higher is Alder?' would have two answers. With a dozen risk factors, it would have thousands.
So let's make a bet instead.
Suppose a risk factor works the same way in every clinic: the same step on the log-odds ruler, wherever you are treated.
Then clinics can differ in only one way: where they start.
Here is that bet as a machine.
One dial, beta, sets the step for everyone. Turn it, and every line tilts together.
And every clinic gets a slider of its own. It moves that clinic's line up or down, and leaves the tilt alone.
We'll call that number gamma.
Statisticians call a line's starting point its intercept.
So that's the whole idea: one intercept per provider, and one shared step.
Written out: a patient's log-odds is their clinic's gamma, plus beta if they are higher-risk.
With more risk factors there are more steps, each with its own beta. There is still just one gamma per clinic.
This is the logistic fixed-effect model.
'Fixed' means only that each gamma is its own unknown number. We assume nothing about how those numbers are spread across clinics.
How the dial and the sliders find their best positions is a story for a later episode. For now, here is where they land.
The shared step is 2.02.
That is the bet at work: in every clinic, higher risk multiplies the odds of readmission by about seven and a half.
Four sliders settle. Birch is lowest, at minus 1.82. Then Cedar. Then Alder and Dune, close together at the top.
Elm's never does. With no readmissions at all, a lower line always fits better, so it slides off the chart.
Elm gets an episode of its own.
Switch to the probability ruler, and the parallel lines become S-curves: one shape, slid sideways.
For a lower-risk patient, the model gives 14% at Birch and 34% at Alder.
For a higher-risk patient, 55% at Birch and 80% at Alder.
One caution. With 103 patients, these are rough estimates. How rough is a question for later.
Notice that the step has grown. The pooled line climbed 1.75. These lines climb 2.02.
Here's why. Each clinic is now compared only with itself: its own higher-risk patients against its own lower-risk patients.
Inside Alder, the step is 2.3. Inside Birch, 1.78. Cedar, 1.79. Dune, 2.3.
Beta is a compromise among those four, weighted by how much each clinic's patients can tell us.
Elm has no say. All of its patients are lower-risk, so it has no step to offer.
Last time, the pooled rule mixed up how sick patients are with where they were treated.
Now the 'where' has a place of its own: the gammas.
That is the first thing we asked for: a risk rule learned from patients who share a clinic.
You might expect one more number: an overall starting point, with each clinic measured from it.
Try it. Raise that number by a half, and lower every gamma by a half.
Nothing on screen moves. The data cannot tell those two descriptions apart, so the model keeps only the gammas.
The same goes for anything that is identical for every patient at a clinic: its size, its ownership, its neighbourhood.
None of them can have a beta of its own. They are already inside gamma.
So what is a gamma? Read it carefully.
Alder's is minus 0.65. That is not a readmission rate. It is a position on the log-odds ruler: the log-odds for a patient with no risk factor switched on.
Here, that's a lower-risk patient at Alder: 34%.
With many risk factors, that patient may not exist at all. So we will mostly read the gaps between gammas, not the gammas themselves.
And gamma is not a pure measure of care.
It holds everything that is constant within a clinic: how well it looks after patients, but also anything about its patients that we failed to measure. The data cannot separate the two.
So read a higher gamma this way: for patients who look the same on paper, more readmissions here than there. Why is a separate question.
Does learning the rule inside providers really help?
Go back to our simulated crowd of 200 providers, where we set the truth ourselves. The true step for the main risk factor is 0.8.
Pool everyone, and the estimate is 0.71, because in this crowd, providers with sicker patients happen to do a little better.
Give every provider its own gamma, and the estimate is 0.81.
Let's gather it up.
Every provider gets its own intercept: gamma.
All providers share one step for each risk factor: beta.
And beta is learned from comparisons inside providers.
Remember what this rests on: the bet that the lines are parallel.
A clinic that does well with lower-risk patients and badly with higher-risk ones would have a line that crosses the others. We will come back and check.
Last time, we asked for two things. The risk rule, we now have.
And the yardstick? Line the gammas up, and one of them sits in the middle: Cedar's.
A middle clinic is a yardstick that no clinic's size can pull toward itself. We'll build on it later.
First, though: Alder's line sits 0.87 above Cedar's. What does that gap mean for an actual patient?
Next time: reading gamma.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
